> A handheld game console I designed from scratch in KiCad. It runs on a bare RP2040 chip instead of a dev board, with a 2-inch 240×320 IPS display, 8 game buttons, an analog thumbstick, and a speaker with its own amplifier. It charges and gets programmed over USB-C. This is my first PCB: a 110 × 60 mm, 2-layer board that I routed by hand with help by Freerouting.

## Design

### 2026-10-08 – 1.

**3h**

1.

Journal of 10/7 (8:00 - 11:00) and 10/8 (5:30 - 7:30)

Post start + goals:
- I have experience in embedded (ranging from Arduino, picos, esp chips)
- I built an 8bit breadboard computer
- I have NO experience in PCB/shipping design. I have made all my projects on breadboards and protoboards.
- Goal: To push my limits and dive deeper into the microcontroller rabbithole (with the obvious goal of learning KiCad)

I wanted to use my 8bit computer idea to build an FPGA (as suggested by hackclub), but I felt this would not be realistic given the short time frame. I was inspired by a handheld game console I made with an Arduino esp32 and a Capacitive touch TFT, so I wanted to build something similar, but everything would be integrated into the microcontroller as a PCB. I chose the RP2040 chip because of its low-cost and high-performance, as well as having used many rp2040 chips in the past.

First Hour:

Installed KiCad 10 and set up the KiCad time tracker. Then, I skimmed the RP2040 datasheet and got an outline on what my project entails:
- Make the controller bootable
- USB and power
- Include the display, buttons, and sound on the GPIO pins.

I an my general plan through AI to verify my idea was realistic, where was helpful in pointing out some gaps in my understanding, as well as suggesting me some specific models of the crystal, USB module, and flash memory.

Started the schematic: Placed the RP2040 and W25Q128JVS (standard 16MB and most supported) flash chip
Wired 6 QSPI lines between them
Powered the flash chip and added a capacitor
Connected the RP2040's 3.3V pins, its 1.1V core pins, and ground

![Screenshot 2026-10-07 214046](https://halflife.hackclub-assets.com/hackclub-half-life/sessions/cRyynVlB17kFXNQz8mUoS9aN3bxNl0uA/ab0b91f89706ffb32edd2ad71141305a2cb1759a7fe4969b7d4517f00920bf50.png)
Problems I encountered:
Never used KiCad before, so these are just UI related problem :
1. Opened find instead of the add-part tool, got stuck in the placing tool
2. A capacitor's ground came loose after moving it. Learned that G drags a part with its wires and M moves it alone
3. KiCad 10 changed its backup settings, I needed the tracker in .zip format

That concluded Hour 1.

Hour 2:

Designed and created both a 1.1V and 3.3V decoupling row, to remove noise

Chose the 4 pin crystal over the 2 pin as the shield would be grounded. 12MHz was the standard.

Problems I encountered:
1. I couldn't see the 4th pin. I had to turn on "show pins" in the menu.
2. Forgot the two load capacitors on the crystal at first. Added a 15pF capacitor from each crystal pin to ground.
3. Put the 1.1V row on a +3.3V symbol by mistake. Learned that KiCad treats +3.3V and +3V3 as two different nets, so the name has to match exactly.

Ad-hoc:

Grounded TESTEN, since it is a factory test pin
Added a BOOTSEL button with a 1k resistor on QSPI_SS.
Added a reset button on RUN
Added a 3 pin debug header (SWCLK, GND, SWDIO) as a backup in case USB doesn't work on my first board

Problems I encountered:
1. I wired one button to both RUN and QSPI_SS, which shorted the two pins together. The chip would have reset every time it read the flash. I had AI review my screenshot and it caught this. Fixed by using two separate buttons.
2. Left the resistors and the crystal with no values. Set them to 1k and 12MHz.
3. Two capacitors were both named C1. Spent 20 minutes going insane figuring out what went wrong here.
4. Needed to add power flags as KiCad was mad at me when I used the ERC.

![Screenshot 2026-10-08 185652](https://halflife.hackclub-assets.com/hackclub-half-life/sessions/cRyynVlB17kFXNQz8mUoS9aN3bxNl0uA/a64cc93b57666f51284e8c7f176bf35ab87afa4777938f970e7584d8021516c1.png)
Hour 3:
Ran ERC

Found RP2040's ground pin was not connected. I had deleted its GND symbol by accident while fixing the other problems
Here's a random thing ERC caught that I would have never saw:
![Screenshot 2026-10-08 193525](https://halflife.hackclub-assets.com/hackclub-half-life/sessions/cRyynVlB17kFXNQz8mUoS9aN3bxNl0uA/543fbf795224e712722cfcf70a46a9604319cc438da6dfd5933780f4da99cf6c.png)

USB and power:
- Placed the USB-C connector, with a 5.1k resistor on each CC pin so chargers recognize the board as a device
- Added 27 ohm resistors on the USB data lines
- Added an AP2112K 3.3V regulator with a 10uF capacitor for stability  on each side, because USB gives 5V and the RP2040 runs on 3.3V

Next log: Add the display, button, joycon and sound. Not sure what model of TFT to use, I'll have to sleep on that!

Hackatime mentions 4 minutes of Claude, that is a background process. Strangely enough, I haven't even made my Kicad project before my time got logged. 1:30hr of pure building were logged, with the other half researching, planning, reading datasheets, and thinking. I'm past the researching stage now, so future logs will have less time dedicated there.
That concluded 10/8.

### 2026-10-10 – Journal of 10/9 (6:25 - 10:25)

**4h**

Journal of 10/9 (6:25 - 10:25)

Finished the whole schematic. Here's what it looks like up until this point. I forgot to commit previously, but I'll try to commit frequently for github in the future.

![image](https://halflife.hackclub-assets.com/hackclub-half-life/sessions/cRyynVlB17kFXNQz8mUoS9aN3bxNl0uA/8eaa9986f60ab9968ac72917f84fafda91f6c087c1a8f2e7bdf369e05b35d487.png)

Buttons and display:

Added 8 push buttons on GPIO2 to GPIO9, each one connecting its pin to ground, for player controllers. Will use the RP2040 has internal pull-ups.
Added a 14 pin connector for the display ribbon and wired the 5 SPI signals to GPIO17 to GPIO21 for the ST7789. My display would be 2.0".
Built the backlight circuit: 47 ohm resistor from 5V, with an NPN transistor switched ON/OFF GPIO22.

![Screenshot 2026-10-09 193452](https://halflife.hackclub-assets.com/hackclub-half-life/sessions/cRyynVlB17kFXNQz8mUoS9aN3bxNl0uA/f151e2c597d486ab956e1db3fcfe66b55b97e4abf16d93a07ecefb04c0611bf6.png)

Problems I encountered:
1. I only wired the display's signal pins and forgot its power and ground. ERC showed 7 unconnected pins on the connector.
2. I had the backlight transistor in backwards (collector to ground). Discovered this through double checking my circuit.
3. My labels were not connected to anything. Learned that a label has to sit exactly on a wire end, and the same name has to appear twice to link two places.
![Screenshot 2026-10-09 194230](https://halflife.hackclub-assets.com/hackclub-half-life/sessions/cRyynVlB17kFXNQz8mUoS9aN3bxNl0uA/44bfeac9631e3870d520b9d55b0d19c522798a59c6d50b3f3786fd5d05477455.png)

Audio:

Decided against a buzzer and an MP3 module (delay, one sound at a time), went with PWM audio into a PAM8302A amplifier so the console can play sounds from the flash.
Added a 10k/1k divider(shrink signal), a 22nF filter capacitor (actually make the sound), and the amp with a speaker connector.
![Screenshot 2026-10-09 202941](https://halflife.hackclub-assets.com/hackclub-half-life/sessions/cRyynVlB17kFXNQz8mUoS9aN3bxNl0uA/30960b2572731665504e39d74d1eb35892ef4c2241f61f28a9a5be350eef8e2a.png)

Problems I encountered:
1. Used the wrong resistance value. Double checked and realized I used 1k where 10k was needed, which would have made the signal too loud.
2. Wired the amp's pull-down resistor in series by mistake.

Thumbstick and expansion header:

The Joy-Con style stick has no datasheet, so all 4 outer ribbon pins go to GPIO26 to GPIO29 through 330 ohm resistors. Firmware will choose which are power, ground, X, and Y.
Added a 6 pin header with serial and I2C for future add-ons like a gyro.
Decided to leave out the SD card, since the 16MB flash is enough.

Had to read the RP2040 datasheet for which pins to use. I avoided pins 0 and 1 as those were debug pins.

ERC is now 0 errors and 0 warnings.
Assigned footprints to every part (0603 for most, 0805 for the larger ones).
![Screenshot 2026-10-09 220352](https://halflife.hackclub-assets.com/hackclub-half-life/sessions/cRyynVlB17kFXNQz8mUoS9aN3bxNl0uA/8ec0f8a424b3d1cde41660222e2149e9768074bfe36ba68480d35196808048b2.png)

Exported the schematic as a PDF and posted it in Slack for review, but no feedback was given.

I'll start board outline, placement, and routing.

That concluded 10/9, but I'm posting this at 10/10 for polishing.

![image](https://halflife.hackclub-assets.com/hackclub-half-life/sessions/cRyynVlB17kFXNQz8mUoS9aN3bxNl0uA/cf9bbb0f5c2adad138b1d2520e7246250aa61c5499cba254d22fd51ac86af45e.png)

Recorded my 5 hour reel from yesterday:
Recorded and posted my progress reel. The decision I reversed was swapping the 40 pin parallel display for a 2 inch SPI panel.

Routing (started):
Routed the crystal: XIN to the crystal and its cap, XOUT through the 1k resistor, then around the crystal to the second cap. The first rout will be the hardest.

Problems I encountered:
1. The RP2040 was rotated 180 degrees, so the crystal pins faced away from the crystal. I only noticed after zooming in and reading the pad names. Fixed the rotation before routing anything else.
2. The crystal was also turned the wrong way at first. It's confusing because most components are upside down in the schematic view. Zooming in shows the pad number/pinout, which is extremely helpful.
3. My first layout packed the crystal parts too tightly to route. I spread them out and manually adjusted their positions by millimeters, making the traces almost straight. I'm extremely proud of my crystal wiring.

### 2026-10-11 – Log 10/11  (12:00 - 1:30)

**1.5h**

Log 10/11  (12:00 - 1:30)

USB
Joined the connector's D- pads and D+ pads with  loops, and made them go through 27 ohm resistors.
![Screenshot 2026-10-11 113256](https://halflife.hackclub-assets.com/hackclub-half-life/sessions/cRyynVlB17kFXNQz8mUoS9aN3bxNl0uA/190fc88ae4e0ae97f29b7b6711447afb6368f998c133265588dfcfedd104c440.png)

Problems I encountered:

After an hour I had 7 connections  and 100+ left, I needed to autoroute to speed up the pace.  Kept the crystal and USB hand-routed, locked them, and used Freerouting for the remaining signals.

Added a slot for the display ribbon and four mounting holes before routing, so traces would avoid them.
The slot was too close to the display connector at first. Moved it so the ribbon has about 4.5mm to bend.

Autorouting:
Exported a DSN file, routed it in Freerouting, imported the results
Added a ground fill on both layers.

First run showed 142 violations. Most came from the edge clearance limit (0.5mm, changed to 0.3mm) and minimum track width.
The rest were cosmetic, so we're fine there

Problems I encountered:
1. Freerouting said only 1 connection was incomplete, but KiCad's rule check found 28. Almost the whole 3.3V supply was unrouted, plus four buttons. The autorouter wasn't always trustable.
![Screenshot 2026-10-11 133421](https://halflife.hackclub-assets.com/hackclub-half-life/sessions/cRyynVlB17kFXNQz8mUoS9aN3bxNl0uA/3e549cb18d34f1195a8eacffcbddda2ffe0e2e009bbec488c42d516c0b869dd1.png)

 A second Freerouting run froze because the ground fill was in the way. Removed the fill to route first and add it back after, still trying to figure this out.

This is getting extremely frustrating, hope I can get the rule check satisfied in the next hour or so. I always have the lock in call! .

I was still looking for the easy way out:

I started with the 3.3V capacitors next to the display connector because they sit close together. I chained C18 to C8 to C7 to C9 to C1, then joined display connector pins 10 and 11, which are both 3.3V. I also joined two pairs of neighboring 3.3V pins on the top row of the chip.

![image](https://halflife.hackclub-assets.com/hackclub-half-life/sessions/cRyynVlB17kFXNQz8mUoS9aN3bxNl0uA/2548c6eb24ace0ffaf8214255c88fc68ad8147b02350dcab1300b8e86b302288.png)

That took the count from 27 down to 18, and then to 14.

![image](https://halflife.hackclub-assets.com/hackclub-half-life/sessions/cRyynVlB17kFXNQz8mUoS9aN3bxNl0uA/eabc8bd66ad8657b039e8f5b005753336c88917c6736f1dc89a00db84e396ef3.png)

The last 14 were the ones the autorouter could not do either, and were by far the hardest.

Chip pin 23 was boxed in by vias the autorouter placed under the chip.
Four button lines (GPIO2, 3, 5 and 8) had no way out from the right side of the chip. I tried SW4 to GPIO2 and could not find a path. All connections were extremely ugly and went through 5+ layers of wires/vias.

![image](https://halflife.hackclub-assets.com/hackclub-half-life/sessions/cRyynVlB17kFXNQz8mUoS9aN3bxNl0uA/11cbe57795affb3aff21c14a707351200405b96234f7879d983c8cae588216a2.png)
![Screenshot 2026-10-11 144701](https://halflife.hackclub-assets.com/hackclub-half-life/sessions/cRyynVlB17kFXNQz8mUoS9aN3bxNl0uA/3a61b485ba2599abacd4477d17b2c6bbe7fd0522c5d57ba80c4345ac1da48c27.png)

I joined Half Life huddle to ask for help. I asked if AI assisted autowiring was allowed. In doing this, I said used  autorouter, which I've noted in previous logs. Normally, this kind of autorouting would lead me to being disqualified, but I was granted an exception by @Shadow. I'm very happy I'm able to continue the project, and I'll make sure to ask in the future before using any assistive tools.

![image](https://halflife.hackclub-assets.com/hackclub-half-life/sessions/cRyynVlB17kFXNQz8mUoS9aN3bxNl0uA/3cc37e3c8c1ea886a01805837c27c999561074e52ea72c04e8fa2ad1288fd40c.png)

There was no easy way to finish the project off but to brute force through the spaghetti wires. I went back to my old board to route everything by hand instead.

To make it easier:

1. Set the grid to 0.05 mm so the cursor can land on exact coordinates.
2. Add track widths of 0.15, 0.2 and 0.4 mm in Pre-defined Sizes, though I mainly used 0.15mm.

Problems I encountered:
1. I didn't really understand how vias worked. They are basically a hole in the circuit board, so pressing V does not just swap colors, you also need 0.15mm clearance between wires.
2. I did not know if I had to route every 3.3V connection. This was very annoying. The regulator's output pin was not connected to anything yet, so nothing on the board would have had power.

After the first wire I decided to use brute force for the final four button lines, pin 23, and all the 3.3V connections. I used a lot of vias to shred through layers of spaghetti that the autorouter made. However, it should be fine, as power should be fine, the only thing I worry is input delay from the button wires. Only USB and the crystal should be clean, and I did those manually.

The last connection:
The rule check said 1 unconnected item: a 3.3V trace on the front and a 3.3V trace on the back. I could not find it by looking, so I saved the DRC report and got the cords of the chip. I was able to see the tiny haywire of a connection, though it still took a ton of time even with the cords.

I still have to add the ground fill (as someone in the huddle suggested), export the gerbers and BOM, and write the firmware and README.

Every connection on the board is routed now. Although the autorouter sped up the process, I learned that its spaghetti wiring that made it difficult to wire the last 27. Never again will I use the autorouter, it's a scam (at least for things of this scope). It would have been easier to wire everything by hand.
